name: Omar Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach youth strings at the arts centre, lead my quartet in rehearsal, and arrange music for small events when a commission comes. I have a music master’s and know my way around a score, but I still like a pencil and a room full of players.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brings you back, and what is hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A child hearing the other strings for the first time is why I stay. The hardest bit is watching the centre discuss cuts without telling teachers which hours are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the string players that a better booking form is useful, but a quartet still has to hear one another. I would keep our Sunday rehearsals exactly where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have about four months of expenses saved, so a cancelled studio call would hurt without breaking me. I worry more about the arts centre cutting its youth orchestra for ordinary budget reasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep leading the youth strings and playing quartet weddings this season. I would send the arts centre a proposed rehearsal calendar before January, as I usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the centre budget, though my own pay is steady enough for now. A quiet wedding month does not send me straight to the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far would your savings take you after a cancelled booking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If one wedding is lost, I can use the savings instead of missing rent. I would still ask the quartet to look for another date because that money takes time to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the arts centre about the youth orchestra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The students need someone to correct a stiff wrist, not just a sheet of notes. I want the arts centre to hear that before it trims the youth programme.

say: I would tell the **quartet** that booking tools may improve while rehearsal stays human.
I would defend the **youth orchestra** at the arts centre.
think: My **four-month cushion** can absorb one lost wedding without missing rent.
An ordinary **arts centre budget cut** still worries me.
do: Keep the **youth strings** and quartet weddings this season.
Send the **rehearsal calendar** to the arts centre before January.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the youth programme, while my own pay is steady.
S0.quote: A quiet wedding month does not send me straight to the landlord.
fieldNote: His **moderate savings** give him room after a lost booking.
He is more concerned with the **youth programme** than a minor change to booking forms.

steps.text: Keep leading youth strings and playing quartet weddings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say at the arts centre that software may write posters, arrange parts and book rooms, and we should discuss what it means for staff hours. I would ask the musicians union to sit in on that talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my small arranging commissions would shrink, and the centre might avoid replacing a departing teacher. Four months of savings buys time, but it does not rebuild a teaching team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the union representative before the next budget meeting and bring the centre’s teaching timetable. In the first year I would keep the youth orchestra rehearsing and ask parents to attend a public budget session if a teacher post is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious because my own arrangement fees could shrink and the teaching hours might be next. I can still plan with the union and the families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your income comes from arrangements?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The commissions are about one tenth of my income in a good term. I would stop promising myself that money for summer travel and keep it in the household account if it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask parents to join the union campaign now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not ask parents to speak unless the centre actually proposes a cut. Otherwise I would show them what the students play, not turn every concert into a meeting.

say: I would ask for a **staff-hours discussion** before the centre changes scheduling and arranging.
I would invite the **musicians union** into that discussion.
think: My **arranging fees** could shrink by about one tenth of good-term income.
A missing **teacher post** would leave the youth programme thinner.
do: Call the **union representative** before the next budget meeting with the timetable.
Invite **parents** to a public budget session if a teacher post is cut.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fees and teaching hours, though I have time to organise.
S1.quote: Four months of savings buys time, but it does not rebuild a teaching team.
fieldNote: His personal **arrangement income** faces thinking AI before live strings do.
He conditions **parent action** on an actual proposed post cut, not a general protest.

steps.text: Call the musicians union before the centre budget meeting
Remove expected arrangement fees from the summer travel budget
Keep youth orchestra rehearsals through the first disruption year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre that AGI by 2028 could produce scores and lesson plans cheaply, but the children deserve a real teacher. I would demand a consultation before any paid hours disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect arrangement fees to go in 2028, and I could lose teaching hours if the centre decides one teacher can supervise a bigger group. Stage robots arrive around 2031; my quartet has longer, but I would not spend the cushion on that hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would collect the last two terms of pay slips and ask the union to compare staff hours. If the centre cuts my hours after 2028, I would apply to two nearby music schools and cut our summer holiday before the savings fall below two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed if my own teaching hours were cut. Until the centre decides, I would be anxious and watch the timetable closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of the cushion would you use before searching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two months of expenses is my line. I would apply before reaching that line, not wait until the account is empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner that you would not say at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner I can cover our rent for a while, but I cannot promise the same pay all year. A senior title will not pay my rent if the arts centre cuts my teaching hours.

say: I would demand **consultation** before the centre removes paid teaching hours.
I would defend **real teachers** for the youth orchestra.
think: My **arrangement fees** could end in 2028, before stage robots around 2031.
A centre decision to enlarge classes could cut **my teaching hours**.
do: Bring two terms of **pay slips** to the union this month.
Apply to **two music schools** if the centre cuts my hours after 2028.
Cut our **summer holiday** if post-2028 centre hours fall and savings approach two months.
feel: I feel **anxious** while hours remain, and alarmed if the centre cuts them.
S2.quote: A senior title will not pay my rent if the arts centre cuts my teaching hours.
fieldNote: He names a **two-month savings floor** before which he would seek another post.
His projected 2028 loss is **arranging work**; larger teaching cuts are a condition, not a certainty.

steps.text: Bring two terms of pay slips to the musicians union
Apply to two music schools if centre hours fall after 2028
Cut summer holiday if centre hours fall after 2028 and savings approach two months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the quartet that AGI by 2031 gives us several seasons to write fair contracts and keep our audiences. I would ask the centre to guarantee a teacher for each youth section for the next term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me save more and find another school if needed. I still think arranging income goes in 2031, and stage robots around 2034 might affect quartet fees, though I do not know what audiences will choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put half of each arrangement commission into savings from next month, while those commissions still exist. Before 2031 I would ask two nearby schools about vacancies, and in the first year after AGI I would keep teaching while checking whether the centre renews my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the commissions, but not trapped. A few years let me make the calls without leaving my pupils suddenly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home if commissions fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would keep the current flat and delay replacing our car if the commissions fall. That is easier than moving the children in the youth orchestra to a different teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What length of guarantee could the centre honestly give?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a one-term guarantee, because the centre can actually approve that. A five-year promise from the arts centre would be pleasant paper, not something I could bank.

say: I would ask the centre for a **one-term teacher guarantee** for each youth section.
I would tell the quartet to plan **fair contracts** across the next seasons.
think: My **arranging income** likely ends in 2031 before possible 2034 stage robots.
Five years gives me time to build **savings** and check nearby schools.
do: Save half of each **arrangement commission** from next month while commissions exist.
Ask **two schools** about vacancies before 2031 and check centre hours afterward.
feel: I feel **anxious** about commissions, but the longer clock gives me room.
S3.quote: A five-year promise from the arts centre would be pleasant paper, not something I could bank.
fieldNote: He asks the centre for a **one-term promise** it can actually approve.
His **commission savings** depend on work that may dry up once thinking AI arrives.

steps.text: Save half of each arrangement commission while commissions still arrive
Ask two nearby schools about teaching vacancies before 2031
Delay replacing the car if arrangement commissions fall
Keep youth string lessons while checking centre hours after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the youth orchestra that AGI by 2036 gives them years to learn the instrument and the work of playing together. I would ask the centre to keep a place for live strings in every season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I might have enough teaching work and savings to live without arrangements. Robots around 2039 could affect stage fees, but I cannot tell whether a wedding party would choose a machine over a quartet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save a portion of each paid commission now and keep teaching at the centre while the youth orchestra is funded. In the first year after 2036 I would review actual quartet bookings each term and ask the union for help if the centre proposes cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about next spring’s budget vote. The long road gives us choices, but a cut could still take away some of my own teaching hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How large a cushion would you want before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My target would be six months of expenses saved before 2036. If the centre cuts hours earlier, I would use that cushion while applying elsewhere, not call it a retirement pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could a live youth orchestra give a child?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children need a room where they can play badly together and improve. An automatic score cannot give a shy violinist another child to listen to.

say: I would ask the centre to preserve **live strings** each season.
I would tell pupils to keep learning **together** through the decade.
think: Six months of **savings** could make lost arranging work survivable by 2036.
I remain unsure how **2039 stage robots** would affect wedding bookings.
do: Save part of each **paid commission** now toward a six-month cushion.
Review **quartet bookings** each term in the first year after 2036.
Ask the **musicians union** for help if the centre proposes cuts after 2036.
feel: I feel **anxious** because an ordinary budget vote could cut my teaching hours next spring.
S4.quote: The children need a room where they can play badly together and improve.
fieldNote: His **six-month goal** is conditional on continued commissions and teaching hours.
The youth orchestra is both **income** and a place where students learn from one another.

steps.text: Save part of each paid commission toward six months of expenses
Keep centre teaching while the youth orchestra is funded

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because arranging fees could disappear before we negotiate the next centre budget. A paid-hours guarantee for the youth programme and a union consultation would help me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the children what a rehearsal gives them that a file cannot. Their answer might make the budget meeting less abstract.

headlineQuote: A child hearing the other strings for the first time is why I stay.
portrait: At **27**, Omar leads youth strings, plays quartet weddings and arranges music with a master’s degree and four months saved.
He resists **AI tools**, trusting live rehearsal, pencil scores and direct teaching instead.
His **union view** leads him to seek consultation and paid-hours evidence before centre staffing changes.
Across AGI dates, he protects **teaching hours** while saving commissions and checking nearby schools if needed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase arrangement fees before Omar and his union secure the next centre budget.
whatWouldHelp: A **youth programme guarantee** and union consultation would let Omar plan around actual paid hours.
